scenes.tts: Two small cells. One is a methane-making microbe, a methanogen. The other is the bacterium Escherichia coli. Under a microscope they look much alike, and neither has a nucleus. Methanogens live in the guts of cattle and humans. Are they close relatives?
scenes.visual: Two identical-looking rod cells, an orange methanogen and a blue E. coli, each labelled no nucleus; a large question mark grows between them.
scenes.narration: Two small cells. One is a methane-making microbe, a methanogen. The other is the bacterium Escherichia coli. Under a microscope they look much alike, and neither has a nucleus. Methanogens live in the guts of cattle and humans. Are they close relatives?

scenes.tts: For a long time, biologists lumped cells with no nucleus together as prokaryotes. That grouping rests on an absence. Two cells that both lack a nucleus need not be close relatives. Every cell has ribosomes, the particles that make proteins. Carl Woese looked for a part that every cell carries. He chose the R N A of the small ribosomal subunit. It is present in all cells, and it does the same job in each.

scenes.visual: A bracket labelled prokaryotes joins the two cells, then breaks into a question; the cells line up with a yeast beside them and a ribosomal RNA bar lights up in all three.

scenes.tts: His laboratory and its collaborators grew microbes. They included typical bacteria and several methane-producing species, called methanogens. They extracted the ribosomal R N A and cut it into short pieces with an enzyme, ribonuclease T one. Then they catalogued the sequence of each piece.

scenes.tts: Each pair of organisms then received a similarity score. The score was higher when their catalogues shared more pieces. Under the old split, methanogens look like bacteria, so they should score closest to other bacteria. They did not.
scenes.visual: Two catalogues linked by shared pieces fill a score meter; then methanogen against bacterium, with a dashed expected mark that the meter fails to reach.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-seven, Woese and George Fox reported that the methanogens formed their own group. It was about as distant from typical bacteria as from the cytoplasmic ribosomal R N A of eukaryotes. They called it the archaebacteria, a third primary kingdom.

scenes.visual: A similarity map: the methanogen dot leaves its expected spot beside bacteria and settles apart, with two equal dashed distances to bacteria and to eukaryotes.
scenes.narration: In 1977, Woese and George Fox reported that the methanogens formed their own group. It was about as distant from typical bacteria as from the cytoplasmic ribosomal RNA of eukaryotes. They called it the archaebacteria, a third primary kingdom.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety, Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis proposed the three domains now in use. They are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Archaea differ from bacteria in more than R N A. Their membrane lipids have ether bonds, and their walls lack peptidoglycan. They are not simply extreme bacteria. The three names are still the standard labels, but recent trees built from many genes nest eukaryotes inside the Asgard archaea. The comparison observed no ancestor, and it did not show how eukaryotic cells arose. It did show that appearance does not reveal deep relationships, and that a shared molecule can.
